Here is a full three-layer GPS classification of every assertion in the project — **source** (original vs. derivative), **information** (primary, secondary, or indeterminate), and **evidence** (direct vs. indirect).

---

## Source Classification

The GPS asks three questions about every source, layered on top of each other.

---

### Layer 1 — Source Type: Original vs. Derivative

| Source | Type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **src_001** — 1850 Census, FamilySearch image | **Original** | A digital image of the actual census schedule as the enumerator recorded it. No intermediate has altered the content. |
| **src_002** — 1850 Census, Ancestry index | **Derivative** | Ancestry's transcription/index of that same census. An intermediary (the transcriber) re-keyed the original. Transcription errors are possible. |
| **src_003** — 1860 Census, FamilySearch image | **Original** | Same logic as src_001 — a digital image of the original schedule. |
| **src_004** — 1908 Death Certificate | **Original** | A government-created record (Pennsylvania Dept. of Health) produced at the time of the event. Even though the informant's knowledge varies by fact, the document itself is original. |

> **Note:** "Original" describes the *source*, not the *quality of knowledge* it contains. An original source can still carry secondary or indeterminate information.

---

### Layer 2 — Information Quality: Primary, Secondary, or Indeterminate

This layer asks: *Who was the informant, and did they have firsthand knowledge of this specific fact at or near the time it occurred?*

**Primary information** (informant had firsthand knowledge, recorded near the event):

| Assertion | Fact | Why primary |
|---|---|---|
| **a_003** | Patrick's residence in 1850, Schuylkill Co., PA | The census enumerator was a *witness* — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. No hearsay needed for the residence fact. |
| **a_011** | Patrick's death, 12 March 1908 | The attending physician signed the death certificate and witnessed the death. Firsthand, contemporaneous. |

---

**Secondary information** (informant lacked firsthand knowledge, or reported long after the event):

| Assertion | Fact | Why secondary |
|---|---|---|
| **a_012** | Patrick born 1845 in Pennsylvania | Reported by son-in-law James Brown in 1908 — 63 years after the birth, to which he was not a witness. He almost certainly learned this secondhand. |
| **a_013** | Father: Thomas Flynn | Same informant (James Brown), reporting his father-in-law's parentage. A son-in-law has no firsthand knowledge of his wife's grandfather's identity. Classic secondary information. |

---

**Indeterminate information** (informant unknown or proximity uncertain):

| Assertion | Fact | Why indeterminate |
|---|---|---|
| **a_001** | Patrick's name (1850 census) | Census does not identify who answered the door. Likely a household member, possibly a neighbor. Cannot be determined. |
| **a_002** | Patrick's age/birthplace (1850 census) | Same unknown informant as a_001 — age and birthplace require someone to report these facts, but we can't establish who. |
| **a_004** | Patrick listed in Thomas Flynn household (1850) | The *relationship* is a researcher inference from household position — no informant reported it at all. The 1850 census has no relationship column. |
| **a_005** | Thomas Flynn's name (1850 census) | As head of household, Thomas likely answered, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant. |

| **a_008** | Patrick's name (1860 census) | Same reasoning as a_001. |
| **a_009** | Patrick's age/birthplace (1860 census) | Same reasoning as a_002. |
| **a_010** | Patrick listed in Thomas Flynn household (1860) | Same reasoning as a_004 — researcher inference; the 1860 census also has no relationship column. |

| **a_013** | Father: Thomas Flynn | **Directly names the father** — the most important direct assertion for q_001 |

**Indirect evidence** (requires an inferential step to connect to the research question):

| Assertion | Fact | Inference required |
|---|---|---|
